key_insight: The paper shows that the preexisting spectral roughness of a finite thermohaline interface can strongly alter salt-finger onset and exchange, so interfacial memory acts like an additional state variable beyond local thermodynamic conditions.
engineering_relevance: For ocean mixing and stratified-flow modeling, this means interface history and roughness spectrum may need to be tracked to better predict exchange rates, plume development, and layer contact timing.
method: Controlled 3D direct numerical simulations of double-diffusive exchange between finite layers.
Held density ratio, diffusivity ratio, Prandtl number, interface thickness, roughness amplitude, domain, resolution, and analysis window fixed.
Varied only the imposed roughness spectrum, with one case repeated using a second realization.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that broad low-mode memory produced the largest cumulative salt exchange and earliest contact, while high-annulus and mixed-memory cases showed distinct, realization-sensitive pathways.
watch_item: The conclusions are based on controlled simulations, so translating spectral-memory effects to real ocean interfaces will require validation against field observations and broader parameter ranges.
paper_title: Interfacial Spectral Memory as a State Variable for Finite-Depth Salt-Finger Exchange
